_meta.title: Spa City Sparkle (match-3) world route
_meta.builtBy: games/match-3 puzzle/tools/build-route.mjs (Spa City Sparkle Phase A)

schema.worlds: array of 6 worlds in play order
schema.world fields: world (1-6), id, name, era (era id; "any" = cross-era), palette (tokens slug), postcard (subject of the world's restored postcard), stops[]
schema.stop fields: order (1-10, the level number), placeId (places.json id or null), name (level name), lat, lng (decimal degrees or null), coordSource ("places.json:<id>" own point, "parent:<id>" the parent place's point used as a stand-in, or "none"), era, fact (one line), source, sourceUrl

notes: Coordinates are copied from research/places.json (whose own coordSource notes apply). A "parent:" coordinate is the containing place (park, lake, mountain or hotel), not the stop itself.
Facts restate research/ topic files; items marked "(added 2026-11-01)" come from the match-3 web research recorded in geography-lakes-mountains.md, other-attractions.md and SOURCES.md.
Stop order is a level order for the game, not a walking or driving route.

worlds.name: Bathhouse Row
worlds.postcard: Bathhouse Row from across Central Avenue: eight facades behind a line of magnolias, Hot Springs Mountain behind

stops.name: Magnolia Promenade
stops.fact: Laid out in the 1890s by Army engineer Robert Stevens with double rows of magnolias; a single row today.

stops.name: Superior Bathhouse
stops.fact: The northernmost bathhouse on the Row (1916), with green tile medallions on its facade.

stops.name: Hale Bathhouse
stops.fact: Built 1892–93, the oldest surviving bathhouse on the Row.

stops.name: Maurice Bathhouse
stops.fact: Built 1911–12; its visible roof sections are covered in green tile.

stops.name: Main Entrance
stops.fact: Two bronze federal eagles mark the 1890s main entrance designed by Robert Stevens.

stops.name: Fordyce Bathhouse
stops.fact: Cost $212,749.55 with fixtures (1914–15), the most elaborate bathhouse on the Row.

stops.name: Quapaw Bathhouse
stops.fact: Built in 1922 on the sites of the Horseshoe and Magnesia bathhouses; crowned by a chevron-tiled dome.

stops.name: Ozark Bathhouse
stops.fact: Built in 1922; twin towers with three-tiered setbacks flank the entrance.

stops.name: Buckstaff Bathhouse
stops.fact: Opened February 1, 1912, and in continuous operation since.

stops.name: Lamar Bathhouse
stops.fact: Its 1923 opening completed Bathhouse Row.

worlds.name: Hot Springs Mountain & the tufa terraces
worlds.postcard: Steam over gray tufa terraces and the Hot Water Cascade, with the Mountain Tower on the ridge above

stops.name: Display Spring
stops.fact: Covered by a grate for decades and uncovered in the 1930s so visitors could see the water in its natural state.

stops.name: Hot Water Cascade
stops.fact: NPS created the Thermal Water Cascade in 1982; a blue-green alga, Phormidium treleasei, grows where spring water meets light and air.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs National Park

stops.name: Tufa Terrace Trail
stops.fact: A 0.3-mile paved trail whose lower section passes the Hot Water Cascade.
stops.source: NPS: Hot Springs & North Mountain Trails

stops.name: Grand Promenade
stops.fact: A half-mile brick National Recreation Trail on the hillside behind the bathhouses, begun in the 1930s.
stops.source: NPS: Hot Springs & North Mountain Trails

stops.name: Noble Fountain
stops.fact: Moved to the Reserve Avenue end of the Grand Promenade in 1957.

stops.name: Ral Spring
stops.fact: A free spring midway up Hot Springs Mountain whose camp of poor health seekers became known as "Ral City."

stops.name: Peak Trail
stops.fact: A 0.6-mile climb at a 12.6% grade, from 644 to 1,044 ft, toward the tower.
stops.source: NPS: Hot Springs & North Mountain Trails

stops.name: Goat Rock
stops.fact: An overlook on North Mountain; the Goat Rock Trail rises from 886 to 1,067 ft.
stops.source: NPS: Hot Springs & North Mountain Trails

stops.name: Gulpha Gorge
stops.fact: The pink-blazed Gulpha Gorge Trail links the campground to the park trail network.
stops.source: NPS: Hot Springs & North Mountain Trails

stops.name: Mountain Tower
stops.fact: The 216-ft lattice steel tower opened June 3, 1983, after the Woolman (1877) and Rix (1906) towers.

worlds.name: Central Avenue at night
worlds.postcard: Central Avenue after dark looking north to the Arlington's twin towers, Medical Arts setbacks and original neon (sign colors are unsourced, so invented)

stops.name: Valley Street
stops.fact: Central Avenue was Valley Street until it was renamed by the late 1870s.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Central Avenue Historic District

stops.name: The Arlington
stops.fact: The third Arlington was built in 11 months and 3 days and completed Nov. 28, 1924, at the Central/Fountain "Y".

stops.name: Southern Club
stops.fact: Built 1893; after a 1927 sale its front was clad in dark Pittsburgh glass (a 1940s storefront per the 1985 district nomination).

stops.name: Ohio Club
stops.fact: Founded in 1905; during Prohibition it officially became the Ohio Cigar Store.

stops.name: Medical Arts Tower
stops.fact: A 16-story Art Deco tower, Arkansas's tallest building from 1930 until 1960.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Medical Arts Building

stops.name: KTHS Ballroom
stops.fact: Radio KTHS ("Kome To Hot Springs") aired its first program Dec. 20, 1924, from the Arlington ballroom.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: KTHS Radio Station

stops.name: Bridge Street
stops.fact: About 98 ft long; Ripley's Believe It or Not called it the shortest street in the world in the 1940s.
stops.source: ACHP: The Hot Springs National Park Visitors Center

stops.name: Park Hotel
stops.fact: A seven-story hotel on Fountain Street that opened in 1930.

stops.name: Fountain Street
stops.fact: NPS says the "alpha" fault that brings the hot water up roughly follows Central Avenue and Fountain Street.

stops.name: The Vapors
stops.fact: Opened in 1960 at 315 Park Avenue; Tony Bennett first sang "I Left My Heart in San Francisco" there in rehearsal.

worlds.name: Oaklawn & the spring-training fields
worlds.postcard: A linen-style card of a racetrack grandstand on a one-mile oval, with a wooden ballpark grandstand inset (generic, no track or team marks)

stops.name: Baseball Grounds
stops.fact: Where A. G. Spalding and Cap Anson brought the Chicago White Stockings to train in 1886.
stops.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: Hot Springs Baseball Grounds

stops.name: Whittington Park
stops.fact: Opened in 1894 with a 260-ft right-field fence; renamed Ban Johnson Park in 1935.

stops.name: Alligator Farm Fence
stops.fact: Babe Ruth's March 17, 1918, home run cleared Whittington Park and landed in the Alligator Farm (later measured at about 573 ft).

stops.name: Majestic Park
stops.fact: The Detroit Tigers made a practice field here in 1908 and the Boston Red Sox built stands in 1909.

stops.name: Fogel Field
stops.fact: Built in 1912 (also called Fordyce Field); Negro league teams, including the Pittsburgh Crawfords, trained here in the 1930s.
stops.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

stops.name: Sam Guinn Field
stops.fact: Built in 1933 at 497 Crescent Avenue to host Negro leagues spring training.

stops.name: Jaycee Field
stops.fact: The Chicago White Sox trained here from 1948 to 1951; Jaycee Park was built on the old Majestic Field site.

stops.name: Glass Grandstand
stops.fact: Oaklawn's 1905 grandstand was glass-enclosed with steam heat, among the first U.S. tracks with either.

stops.name: Backstretch Chute
stops.fact: The one-mile dirt oval has a backstretch chute for six-furlong sprints.

stops.name: Derby Day
stops.fact: The first Arkansas Derby was run at Oaklawn in 1936 for a purse of $5,000.

worlds.name: Lake Hamilton & Lake Ouachita
worlds.postcard: Lake Ouachita at sunset: pine-covered islands, a pontoon boat and a quartz-flecked shore

stops.name: Carpenter Dam
stops.fact: Begun by Arkansas Power & Light in 1929 and completed in 1931, creating Lake Hamilton.

stops.name: Lake Hamilton
stops.fact: About 7,200 acres, named for Hamilton Moses of Arkansas Power & Light.

stops.name: Hulsey Hatchery
stops.fact: The Andrew Hulsey State Fish Hatchery sits on the south side of Lake Hamilton, its water source.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: AGFC State Fish Hatcheries

stops.name: Remmel Dam
stops.fact: A 1924 Ambursen flat-slab buttress dam that forms Lake Catherine.

stops.name: Catherine's Cabins
stops.fact: The Civilian Conservation Corps built Lake Catherine State Park in the 1930s, including stone-and-wood cabins.

stops.name: Blakely Mountain Dam
stops.fact: The Corps of Engineers built the 231-ft dam from 1948 to 1953, creating Lake Ouachita.

stops.name: Three Sisters Springs
stops.fact: Historic healing springs preserved in Lake Ouachita State Park (opened 1955).

stops.name: Geo-Float Trail
stops.fact: A 16-mile water trail from Spillway to Brady Mountain recreation areas, certified a National Recreation Trail in 1980 (added 2026-11-01).
stops.source: National Recreation Trails: Ouachita Geo-Float Trail

stops.name: Two Hundred Islands
stops.fact: Lake Ouachita has about 200 islands and "one of the largest crystal veins in the world."

stops.name: Mount Ida Crystals
stops.fact: Mount Ida claims the title "Quartz Crystal Capital of the World" and hosts a crystal dig the second week of October (added 2026-11-01).
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: World Championship Quartz Crystal Dig

worlds.name: Garvan Gardens & the revival
worlds.postcard: Anthony Chapel among tall pines above Lake Hamilton, framed by tulips; a restored Bathhouse Row strip along the bottom

stops.name: Fordyce Visitor Center
stops.fact: Closed in 1962 and reopened as the park visitor center on May 13, 1989.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs National Park

stops.name: Quapaw Baths
stops.fact: Restored by NPS in 2004; Quapaw Baths & Spa opened in July 2008.

stops.name: Running of the Tubs
stops.fact: Since 2006, teams have pushed bathtubs the length of Bathhouse Row.
stops.source: Visit Hot Springs: Running of the Tubs 2026 press release

stops.name: Ozark Cultural Center
stops.fact: Reopened in 2014 as the Hot Springs National Park Cultural Center.

stops.name: Hotel Hale
stops.fact: Now Hotel Hale, nine suites with thermal-water soaking tubs (opened May 2019).

stops.name: Maurice Restoration
stops.fact: A $31.6 million rehabilitation broke ground Aug. 19, 2025, the last on the Row.
stops.source: NPS: Groundbreaking celebrated for Maurice Bathhouse rehabilitation

stops.name: Garden of the Pine Wind
stops.fact: A Japanese rock-and-stream garden begun in March 2000 (added 2026-11-01).
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Garvan Woodland Gardens

stops.name: Bridge of the Full Moon
stops.fact: A stone bridge with a round arch, focal point of the Garden of the Pine Wind (via search summary, added 2026-11-01).

stops.name: Anthony Chapel
stops.fact: A wood-and-glass chapel with a 57-ft ceiling on pine columns, opened September 2006.
stops.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Garvan Woodland Gardens

stops.name: Holiday Lights
stops.fact: Visit Hot Springs lists about 5 million lights over 18 acres (earlier counts were about 4 million).
stops.source: Visit Hot Springs: Garvan Woodland Gardens
